extracted.intended_audience: employers (including small businesses), state/local/tribal governments, labor practitioners, and stakeholders participating in notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytical criteria used in the Department of Labor's final rule preamble to estimate impacts on small entities, choose salary/HCE thresholds, assess recordkeeping and compliance burdens, and satisfy RFA/UMRA requirements for a notice-and-comment rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of affected EAP workers to small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate the probability that an exempt EAP worker in the CPS data is employed by a small entity, the Department assumed this probability is equal to the proportion of all workers employed by small entities in the corresponding industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If 50 percent of workers in an industry are employed in small entities, then on average small entities are expected to employ one out of every two exempt EAP workers in this industry. These probabilities are applied to the population of exempt EAP workers to estimate counts employed by small entities. Rationale: no data distinguishing small vs non-small employment of exempt/affected EAP workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume identical small/non-small employment rates when no data exist
rubrics_metrics.description: No data are available to determine whether small businesses are more or less likely than non-small businesses to employ exempt or affected EAP workers; therefore, assign the same rates to all small and non-small businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as the 'best assumption available' in absence of disaggregated data; acknowledge resulting uncertainty in estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper- and lower-bound methods for number of affected small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate a range for affected small entities using two bounding assumptions: (1) upper-end: each small entity employs no more than one affected worker; (2) lower-end: assume affected small entity size equals average small entity size and all employees are affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upper-end yields the maximum number of affected small entities (but minimizes per-entity cost). Lower-end yields the fewest affected entities but largest per-entity impacts. Present both to characterize the range of potential effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average small entity size calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: The average number of employees in a small entity is calculated as the number of workers that small entities employ divided by the total number of small establishments in that industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this average to divide affected employees at small businesses to calculate the lower-range estimate of affected small entities when assuming all employees at an establishment are affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of impacts to estimate for small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate regulatory familiarization costs, adjustment costs, managerial costs, and payroll increases borne by employers for small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide separate estimates for entities with affected employees and those without (who incur only familiarization costs). Summarize impacts by industry and employer type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presenting ranges and per-entity averages
rubrics_metrics.description: Report total direct employer costs as ranges and provide average cost per affected entity and average familiarization cost per non-affected entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example metrics included: total direct employer costs to affected small entities in Year 1 ($368.7M to $443.6M) and average cost per entity ($282 to $1,771); regulatory familiarization costs for non-affected small entities ($274.9M to $349.7M; average $54.82 per entity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of disproportionate burden and mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge small entities may face disproportionately large costs due to limited HR staff, but expect reliance on compliance assistance materials and existing systems for hours/pay monitoring to mitigate burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the narrow scope of changes (salary component only) and existing nonexempt workforce/policies reduce expected burdens on small businesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of an earnings model for estimated employee wage changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Average weekly earnings for affected EAP workers in small entities are estimated using the incomplete fixed-job model referenced in section VII.C.4.iii.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example result: expected average weekly earnings increase of about $7.06 per week per affected worker in small entities, leading to aggregate annual wage payments. Cite the model used and location in the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare costs to payroll and approximate revenues
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess burden by comparing combined costs and payroll increases to average entity payroll and to approximate entity revenues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximate revenues per affected small establishment by multiplying average small entity payroll by the ratio of small business revenues to payroll from SUSB data. Use these percentages to judge materiality (e.g., costs as percent of payroll or revenues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Project multi-year impacts with same methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Project costs and affected workers for Years 2–10 using the same methodology as Year 1, accounting for automatic updates that change affected counts over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report selected years (e.g., Year 1 and Year 10) and provide time series (tables, figures) illustrating how affected worker counts and costs change, noting decreases between update years and increases in updating years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping implications under FLSA/part 516
rubrics_metrics.description: Although no new recordkeeping requirements are introduced, employers will need to keep additional records for employees who become newly nonexempt if they do not presently record such information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite section 11(c) of the FLSA and part 516 regulations; incorporate these burdens into the PRA (Paperwork Reduction Act) analysis and estimate employer burden accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steps to minimize significant economic impact on small entities (RFA compliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the steps taken to minimize economic impacts consistent with the FLSA objectives, including factual, policy, and legal reasons for selected standards and why alternatives were rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explanation of chosen salary/HCE levels, why multiple thresholds (by region/industry/size) are not adopted, and how the selected methodology accommodates small employers and low-wage industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for setting the standard salary level
rubrics_metrics.description: Set the standard salary level equal to the 35th percentile of earnings of full-time salaried workers in the lowest-wage Census Region (the South), resulting in $1,128 per week based on 2023 data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify: restores the salary screening function, sits above the long test salary level but below the short test, reasonably distributes impacts between employees and employers in a one-test system, and avoids multiple regional/industry/size thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for setting the HCE total annual compensation level
rubrics_metrics.description: Set the HCE (highly compensated employee) total annual compensation level equal to the 85th percentile of earnings of full-time salaried workers nationally ($151,164 annually based on 2023 data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify: avoids costs associated with evaluating many highly-paid white-collar employees under the duties test and complements a more lenient HCE duties test; compare to prior rules' percentiles and coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: No differing compliance or reporting requirements for small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: This rule provides no differing compliance and reporting requirements for small entities; the Department will not implement size-based exemptions or different reporting obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: differing requirements would undermine FLSA's uniform floor; the Department instead offers compliance assistance resources and avoids prescriptive record forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarification/consolidation/simplification of reporting where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department does not impose new reporting requirements and strives to minimize respondent recordkeeping burden by requiring no specific form or order of records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize available resources to employers to understand obligations and achieve compliance. Incorporate into RFA discussion of alternatives (603(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow performance-based compliance approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers may achieve compliance through various means (adjust salary levels, hire additional workers, spread overtime hours, or compensate employees for overtime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects a preference for flexible, performance-based compliance rather than prescriptive design standards; list options and associated implications for costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting an exemption for small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: An exemption from coverage for businesses with as many as 500 employees or other small-business thresholds is inconsistent with the FLSA and therefore not adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain statutory incompatibility and note stakeholder input but justify non-selection of exemption alternative under RFA.

rubrics_metrics.name: UMRA written statement requirements for federal mandates
rubrics_metrics.description: When a rule may result in increased expenditures by the private sector or by state/local/tribal governments of $200 million or more in at least one year, UMRA requires a written statement that: (1) identifies authorizing legislation; (2) presents estimated costs and benefits and effects on the national economy; (3) summarizes and evaluates government input; and (4) identifies reasonable alternatives and explains selection/non-selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include tabular Year 1 cost estimates by employer type and explain whether macroeconomic analysis is warranted per OMB guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold for conducting macroeconomic analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Per OMB guidance, macroeconomic effects tend to be measurable only if the regulation's economic effect reaches 0.25–0.5 percent of GDP (approx. $68.4B–$136.8B using 2023 GDP); otherwise a full macro-economic analysis is unlikely to show measurable effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If aggregate costs are below that threshold and not highly geographically or sectorally concentrated, compare costs to payroll and revenues instead of conducting a full macroeconomic model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stakeholder input and consider delayed applicability when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize state/local/tribal government input and consider adjustments such as delayed applicability dates to mitigate impacts (e.g., new thresholds effective Jan 1, 2025).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document listening sessions and comments, describe reasons for accommodations (e.g., predictability, ability to adjust budgets), and incorporate commenter concerns into final rule decisions where warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability of regulatory provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Add a severability provision: provisions of part 541 are separate and severable and operate independently; if any provision is held invalid or unenforceable, construe to give maximum effect permitted by law or sever the provision if utterly invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit regulatory text (§541.5) to preserve remainder of part 541 in event of judicial or administrative invalidation of any provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary thresholds, territory adjustments, and pay-period translations as regulatory requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory text (§541.600) specifies standard salary levels with effective dates (e.g., $844/week beginning July 1, 2024; $1,128/week beginning Jan 1, 2025; level per §541.607(b)(1) as of July 1, 2027), and lower weekly thresholds for certain U.S. territories (e.g., $455/week for Puerto Rico, Guam, CNMI; $380/week for American Samoa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include translation guidance for biweekly, semimonthly, or monthly pay periods (examples provided). These are binding qualifications for exemption under section 13(a)(1).
